cards.explanation: The answer is twelve, friends. Manasseh, Hezekiah's son, is twelve years old when he becomes king, and he reigns in Jerusalem fifty-five years. TWELVE! Some folks can't be trusted with a kitchen timer, and this young man gets a whole kingdom.

The answer is fifty-five years, friends! Manasseh reigns in Jerusalem longer than anyone would guess from a twelve-year-old with a crown. His father Hezekiah, the king before him, reigned twenty-nine years (2 Chronicles 32:33; 29:1). So Manasseh nearly doubles his father's run. That's a lot of mornings on one throne.

The answer is rebuilt, friends. His father Hezekiah tore the high places down, and Manasseh builds them right back up. That's like sweeping the whole counter spotless and then someone tips a tray of crumbs over it before you can put the broom down. One man does the cleanup and the next one undoes it.

The answer is True, friends. The verse says he raised up altars for the Baals and made Asherah poles, along with rebuilding the high places. Verse 2 says he followed the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites. Manasseh is stacking one wrong thing on top of another.

The answer is in both of its courtyards, friends. The verse says, “In both courtyards of the house of the LORD, he built altars to all the host of heaven.” That means these altars sit right inside the LORD's house, in two places. So they aren't in just one spot.

The answer is False, friends. Manasseh doesn't stay away from any of it. The verse says he practiced sorcery, divination, and witchcraft, and consulted mediums and spiritists. It's a heavy part of the story, and the verse says it plainly.

The answer is that they carefully do all He commanded through Moses, friends. God spoke to David, Israel's king, and his son Solomon, and said He would never again cause the Israelites to leave the land, “…if only they are careful to do all that I have commanded them through Moses…” The promise comes with a "carefully do" attached. Manasseh leads the people the other way.

The answer is that their evil is greater, friends. The verse says, “So Manasseh led the people of Judah and Jerusalem astray, so that they did greater evil than the nations that the LORD had destroyed before the Israelites.” That's a heavy line, and the text says it plainly. I think this one hurts.

The answer is False, friends. The verse says the LORD brought against them the military commanders of the king of Assyria. Egypt isn't in this verse at all. Just a good reminder to read the name on the uniform.

The answer is Babylon, friends. It surprised me too, since the commanders serve Assyria's king. But the verse says plainly that they took him to Babylon. I'd have guessed a different city, and I'd have been wrong too.

The answer is humbles, friends. In his distress, Manasseh seeks the favor of the LORD his God and earnestly humbles himself before the God of his fathers. This is the turning point of his whole story. The man who once built altars in the LORD's house now bows low.

The answer is True, friends. The verse says when Manasseh prayed to Him, the LORD received his plea and heard his petition. After all that Manasseh did, God still hears him. That's worth sitting with for a second.

The answer is back to Jerusalem and his kingdom, friends. The verse says the LORD received his plea and brought him back there. A man in a hook and bronze shackles ends up home on his throne. That's a long way from where he started.
The answer is that the LORD is God, friends. The verse says, “Then Manasseh knew that the LORD is God.” Not a bigger palace or a new crown. The big thing he comes to know is the LORD.

The answer is False, friends. Manasseh removed the foreign gods and the idol from the house of the LORD, along with the altars he built, and he dumped them outside the city. Nothing goes to his palace. He cleans house.

The answer is True, friends. After he restored the altar of the LORD and offered peace offerings and thank offerings, he told Judah to serve the LORD, the God of Israel. He had led them astray before. Now he points them the other way.

The answer is only to the LORD their God, friends. The verse says the people still sacrificed at the high places, “…but only to the LORD their God.” So the sacrifices are going to the right One. The high places are still there, and that's what the Nevertheless is pointing at.

The answer is two years, friends. Amon, Manasseh's son, reigns in Jerusalem just two years. After his father's fifty-five, that's barely long enough to get comfortable on the throne. It's a short reign and a hard one.

The answer is increases, friends. The verse says Amon did not humble himself before the LORD as his father Manasseh had done. Instead, he increased his guilt. His father humbled himself, and Amon went the other direction.
The answer is his son Josiah, friends. The people of the land make Josiah king in Amon's place. Amon's story ends hard, and a new king steps in. I'd say that story isn't over.
